native_routines_run: 0x18de3e0 held release body (token load, free-list push, count decrement, held clear)
supplied: 0x143d1de3a protected guard leave (rcx = guard, rdx = pool)
method: Held release 0x18de3e0 run natively with the two guard thunks hooked as recording services that return to the native caller. The Python reference release_pose_link_held runs on copies of the same bytes. A null token is run natively too: the store to address 0 faults, which must match the Python ValueError at the same point after enter.
comparisons: enter and leave call order with arguments (guard value, pool pointer)
final 0x90-byte link bytes, 0x40-byte pool bytes and every token object
fault versus no-fault for the null token, with the pool and link unchanged
coverage: held token 0 in 1 of 8 trials (null fault path)
pool free-list head null in about 30 percent of trials, nonnull otherwise
live count 0 (wraps to 0xffffffff), 1, 2, 7, 0xffffffff and random values
limits: Both guard thunks are protected obfuscated code and are supplied; their lock behavior and any memory they touch are not modeled.
The pool global values are fixtures; the native code reads the guard global before enter and the pool global after enter, and the model takes both as arguments.
Pool free-list heads point to fixture token objects only; no real pool layout beyond +0x28 and +0x30 is modeled.
No live validation, no concurrent release, no evidence about how the caller guarantees a nonzero token beyond the dynamic handler check.
